She has already long ago been disgraced, and has fallen into contempt, among her neighbours (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.57">v. 57</reference>): <hi type="italic">Before her wickedness was discovered,</hi> before she came to be so grossly and openly flagitious, she bore the just punishment of her secret and more concealed lewdness, when she fell under <hi type="italic">the reproach of the daughters of Syria, of the Philistines,</hi> who were said to <hi type="italic">despise her</hi> and <hi type="italic">be ashamed of her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.27">v. 27</reference>), and under the reproach of <hi type="italic">all that were round about her,</hi> which seems to refer to the descent made upon Judah by the Syrians in the days of Ahaz, and soon after another by the Philistines, <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.5">2 Chron. xxviii. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.18">18</reference>. Note, Those that disgrace themselves by yielding to their lusts will justly be brought into disgrace by being made to yield to their enemies; and it is observable that before God brought potent enemies upon them, for <hi type="italic">their destruction,</hi> he brought enemies upon them that were less formidable, <hi type="italic">for their reproach.</hi> If less judgments would do the work, God would not send greater. In this <hi type="italic">thou hast borne thy lewdness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.58">v. 58</reference>. Those that will not cast off their sins by repentance and reformation shall be made to bear their sins to their confusion. (2.) She is now <hi type="italic">in captivity,</hi> or hastening into captivity, and therein is reckoned with, not only for her lewdness (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.58">v. 58</reference>), but for her perfidiousness and covenant-breaking (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.59">v. 59</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will deal with thee as thou hast done;</hi> I will forsake thee as thou hast forsaken me, and cast thee off as thou hast cast me off, for thou hast <hi type="italic">despised the oath, in breaking the covenant.</hi>" This seems to be meant of the covenant God made with their fathers at Mount Sinai, whereby he took them and theirs to be a peculiar people to himself. They flattered themselves with a conceit that because God had hitherto continued his favour to them, notwithstanding their provocations, he would do so still. "No," says God, "you have <hi type="italic">broken covenant with me,</hi> have despised both the promises of the covenant and the obligations of it, and therefore I will <hi type="italic">deal with thee as thou hast done.</hi>" Note, Those that will not adhere to God as their God have no reason to expect that he should continue to own them as his people. (3.) The captivity of the wicked Jews, and their ruin, shall be as irrevocable as that of Sodom and Samaria. In this sense, as a threatening, most interpreters take <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.53">v. 53</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.55">55</reference>. "<hi type="italic">When I shall bring again the captivity of Sodom and Samaria, and when they shall return to their former estate, then I will bring again the captivity of thy captives in the midst of them,</hi> and as it were for their sakes, and under their shadow and protection, because they are <hi type="italic">more righteous than thou,</hi> and <hi type="italic">then thou shalt return to thy former estate,</hi>" But Sodom and Samaria were never brought back, nor ever returned to their former estate, and therefore let not Jerusalem expect it, that is, those who now remained there, whom God would <hi type="italic">deliver to be removed into all the kingdoms of the earth for their hurt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.24.9-Jer.24.10">Jer. xxiv. 9, 10</reference>. Sooner shall the Sodomites arise out of the salt sea, and the Samaritans return out of the land of Assyria, than they enjoy their peace and prosperity again; for, to their shame be it spoken, it is <hi type="italic">a comfort</hi> to those of the ten tribes, who are dispersed and in captivity, to see those of the two tribes who had been as bad as they, or worse, in like manner dispersed and in captivity; and therefore they shall live and die, shall stand and fall, together. The bad ones of both shall perish together; the good ones of both shall return together. Note, Those who do as the worst of sinners do must expect to fare as they fare. <hi type="italic">Let my enemy be as the wicked.</hi>
entries.ae0fac3d1458e255fa42130339053cbdc142b5d2: <div eID="gen18701" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Mercy in Reserve; Promise of Mercy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 593.)</title> <div sID="gen18702" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">60</hi> Nevertheless I will remember my covenant with thee in the days of thy youth, and I will establish unto thee an everlasting covenant. <hi type="super">61</hi> Then thou shalt remember thy ways, and be ashamed, when thou shalt receive thy sisters, thine elder and thy younger: and I will give them unto thee for daughters, but not by thy covenant. <hi type="super">62</hi> And I will establish my covenant with thee; and thou shalt know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="super">63</hi> That thou mayest remember, and be confounded, and never open thy mouth any more because of thy shame, when I am pacified toward thee for all that thou hast done, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen18702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18703" type="x-p"/> Here, in the close of the chapter, after a most shameful conviction of sin and a most dreadful denunciation of judgments, mercy is remembered, mercy is reserved, for those who shall come after. As was when God swore in his wrath concerning those who came out of Egypt that they should not enter Canaan, "Yet" (says God) "your little ones shall;" so here. And some think that what is said of the return of Sodom and Samaria (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.53">v. 53</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.55">55</reference>), and of Jerusalem with them, is a promise; it may be understood so, if by Sodom we understand (as Grotius and some of the Jewish writers do) the Moabites and Ammonites, the posterity of Lot, who once dwelt in Sodom; their captivity was returned (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.47">Jer. xlviii. 47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.6">xlix. 6</reference>), as was that of many of the ten tribes, and Judah's with them. But these closing verses are, without doubt, a previous promise, which was in part fulfilled at the return of the penitent and reformed Jews out of Babylon, but was to have its full accomplishment in gospel-times, and in that <hi type="italic">repentance and</hi> that <hi type="italic">remission of sins</hi> which should then be <hi type="italic">preached</hi> with success <hi type="italic">to all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.</hi> Now observe here, <div eID="gen18703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18704" type="x-p"/> I. Whence this mercy should take rise-from <hi type="italic">God himself,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">remembering his covenant</hi> with them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.60">v. 60</reference>): <hi type="italic">Nevertheless,</hi> though they had been so provoking, and God had been provoked to such a degree that one would think they could never be reconciled again, yet "<hi type="italic">I will remember my covenant with thee,</hi> that covenant which I made with thee <hi type="italic">in the days of thy youth,</hi> and will revive it again. Though thou hast <hi type="italic">broken the covenant</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.59">v. 59</reference>), I will remember it, and it shall flourish again." See how much it is our comfort and advantage that God is pleased to deal with us in a covenant-way, for thus the mercies of it come to be <hi type="italic">sure mercies</hi> and <hi type="italic">everlasting</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa. lv. 3</reference>); and, while this root stands firmly in the ground, there is <hi type="italic">hope of the tree,</hi> though it be <hi type="italic">cut down,</hi> that <hi type="italic">through the scent of water it will bud again.</hi> We do not find that they put him in mind of the covenant, but <hi type="italic">ex mero motu—from his own mere good pleasure,</hi> he <hi type="italic">remembers</hi> it as he had promised. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.42">Lev. xxvi. 42</reference>, <hi type="italic">Then will I remember my covenant, and will remember the land.</hi> He that bids us to be ever mindful of the covenant no doubt will himself be ever mindful of it, the word <hi type="italic">which he commanded</hi> (and what he commands stands fast for ever) to <hi type="italic">a thousand generations.</hi> <div eID="gen18704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18705" type="x-p"/> II. How they should be prepared and qualified for this mercy (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.61">v. 61</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt remember thy ways,</hi> thy evil ways; God will put thee in mind of them, will set them in order before thee, that thou mayest be <hi type="italic">ashamed of them.</hi>" Note, God's good work in us commences and keeps pace with his good-will towards us. When he remembers his covenant for us, that he may not remember our sins against us, he puts us upon remembering our sins against ourselves. And if we will but be brought to remember our ways, how crooked and perverse they have been and how we have walked contrary to God in them, we cannot but be ashamed; and, when we are so, we are best prepared to receive the honour and comfort of a sealed pardon and a settled peace. <div eID="gen18705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18706" type="x-p"/> III. What the mercy is that God has in reserve for them. 1. He will take them into covenant with himself (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.60">v. 60</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will establish unto thee an everlasting covenant;</hi> and again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.62">v. 62</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will establish,</hi> re-establish, and establish more firmly than ever, <hi type="italic">my covenant with thee.</hi> Note, It is an unspeakable comfort to all true penitents that the covenant of grace is so well ordered in all things that every transgression in the covenant does not throw us out of the covenant, for that is inviolable. 2. He will bring the Gentiles into church-communion with them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.61">v. 61</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt receive thy sisters,</hi> the Gentile nations that are found about thee, <hi type="italic">thy elder and thy younger,</hi> greater than thou art and less, ancient nations and modern, and <hi type="italic">I will give them unto thee for daughters;</hi> they shall be founded, nursed, taught, and educated, by that gospel, that <hi type="italic">word of the Lord,</hi> which shall <hi type="italic">go forth from</hi> Zion and from <hi type="italic">Jerusalem;</hi> so that all the neighbours shall call Jerusalem <hi type="italic">mother,</hi> while the church continues there, and shall acknowledge the Jerusalem which is from above, and <hi type="italic">which is free,</hi> to be <hi type="italic">the mother of us all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.26">Gal. iv. 26</reference>. They shall be thy <hi type="italic">daughters,</hi> but <hi type="italic">not by thy covenant,</hi> not by the covenant of peculiarity, not as being proselytes to the Jewish religion and subject to the yoke of the ceremonial law, but as being converts with thee to the Christian religion." Or <hi type="italic">not by thy covenant</hi> may mean, "not upon such terms as thou shalt think fit to impose upon them as conquered nations, as captives and homagers to whom thou mayest give law at pleasure" (such a dominion as that the carnal Jews hope to have over the nations); "no, they shall be thy daughters <hi type="italic">by my covenant,</hi> the covenant of grace made with thee and them in concert, as in <hi type="italic">indenture tripartite.</hi> I will be a Father, a common Father, both to Jews and Gentiles, and so they shall become sisters to one another. And, when thou <hi type="italic">shalt receive them,</hi> thou shalt be <hi type="italic">ashamed of thy own evil ways</hi> wherein thou wast conformed to them. Thou shalt blush to look a Gentile in the face, remembering how much worse than the Gentiles thou wast in the day of thy apostasy." <div eID="gen18706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18707" type="x-p"/> IV. What the fruit and effect of this will be. 1. God will hereby be glorified (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.62">v. 62</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt know that I am the Lord.</hi> It shall hereby be known that the God of Israel is Jehovah, a God of power, and faithful to his covenant; and thou shalt know it who hast hitherto lived as if thou didst not know or believe it." It had often been said in wrath, <hi type="italic">You shall know that I am the Lord,</hi> shall know it to your cost; here it is said in mercy, You shall know it to your comfort; and it is one of the most precious promises of the new covenant which God has made with us that <hi type="italic">all shall know him from the least to the greatest.</hi> 2. They shall hereby be more humbled and abased for sin ( <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.63">v. 63</reference>): "<hi type="italic">That thou mayest be</hi> the more <hi type="italic">confounded</hi> at the <hi type="italic">remembrance of all that thou hast done</hi> amiss, mayest reproach thyself for it and call thyself a thousand times unwise, undutiful, ungrateful, and unlike what thou wast, and mayest never <hi type="italic">open thy mouth any more</hi> in contradiction to God, reflection on him, or complaints of him, but mayest be for ever silent and submissive <hi type="italic">because of thy shame.</hi>" Note, Those that rightly remember their sins will be truly ashamed of them; and those that are truly ashamed of their sins will see great reason to be patient under their afflictions, to be dumb, and not open their mouths against what God does. But that which is most observable is, that all this shall be <hi type="italic">when I am pacified towards thee, saith the Lord God.</hi> Note, It is the gracious ingenuousness of true penitents that the clearer evidences and the fuller instances they have of God's being reconciled to them the more grieved and ashamed they are that ever they have offended God. God is in Jesus Christ <hi type="italic">pacified towards us;</hi> he is our peace, and it is by his cross that we are reconciled, and in his gospel that God is reconciling the world to himself. Now the consideration of this should be powerful to melt our hearts into a godly sorrow for sin. This is repenting because <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven is at hand.</hi> The prodigal, after he had received the kiss which assured him that his father was <hi type="italic">pacified towards him,</hi> was ashamed and confounded, and said, <hi type="italic">Father, I have sinned against heaven and before thee.</hi> And the more our shame for sin is increased by the sense of pardoning mercy the more will our comfort in God be increased.  <chapter eID="Ezek.16"/> <div eID="gen18707" type="x-p"/>

entries.86f878d46156868e9a08144a19aacbc7cb8c63f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11204"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.16.1-Ezek.16.63">Eze 16:1-63</reference>. Detailed Application of the Parabolical Delineation of the Fifteenth Chapter to Jerusalem Personified as a Daughter.</title> <div sID="gen20209" type="x-p"/> (1) Taken up by God's gratuitous favor from infancy (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.1-Ezek.7.2">Eze 16:1-7); (2</reference>) and, when grown up, joined to Him in spiritual marriage (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.8-Ezek.14.3">Eze 16:8-14); (3</reference>) her unfaithfulness, her sin (Eze 16:15-34); (4) the judgment (Eze 16:35-52); (5) her unlooked-for restoration (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.53">Eze 16:53</reference> to the close).<div eID="gen20209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20210" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11204"/><hi type="bold">2. cause Jerusalem to know--</hi>Men often are so blind as not to perceive their guilt which is patent to all. "Jerusalem" represents the whole kingdom of Judah. <div eID="gen20210" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ab2476c9d627a430f985a76751ccd26dcf7dfe4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11205"/><div sID="gen20211" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11205"/><hi type="bold">3. birth ... nativity--</hi>thy origin and birth; literally, "thy diggings" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.51.1">Is 51:1</reference>) "and thy bringings forth."<div eID="gen20211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of ... Canaan--</hi>in which Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob sojourned before going to Egypt, and from which thou didst derive far more of thy innate characteristics than from the virtues of those thy progenitors (<reference osisRef="Ezek.21.30">Eze 21:30</reference>).<div eID="gen20212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20213" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">an Amorite ... an Hittite--</hi>These, being the most powerful tribes, stand for the whole of the Canaanite nations (compare <reference osisRef="Josh.1.4">Jos 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.2.9">Am 2:9</reference>), which were so abominably corrupt as to have been doomed to utter extermination by God (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.24">Le 18:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.28">25, 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.12">De 18:12</reference>). Translate rather, "the Amorite ... the Canaanite," that is, these two tribes personified; their wicked characteristics, respectively, were concentrated in the parentage of Israel (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Ge 15:16</reference>). "The Hittite" is made their "mother"; alluding to Esau's wives, daughters of Heth, whose ways vexed Rebekah (<reference osisRef="Gen.26.34">Ge 26:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.26.35">35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.27.46">27:46</reference>), but pleased the degenerate descendants of Jacob, so that these are called, in respect of morals, children of the Hittite (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.45">Eze 16:45</reference>). <div eID="gen20213" type="x-p"/>
entries.83b82c3ee0489fcc1362305c84ab0f10ce07612d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11206"/><div sID="gen20214" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11206"/>4. Israel's helplessness in her first struggling into national existence, under the image of an infant (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.3">Ho 2:3</reference>) cast forth without receiving the commonest acts of parental regard. Its very life was a miracle (<reference osisRef="Exod.1.15-Exod.1.22">Ex 1:15-22</reference>).<div eID="gen20214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">navel ... not cut--</hi>Without proper attention to the navel cord, the infant just born is liable to die.<div eID="gen20215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither ... washed in water to supple thee--</hi>that is, to make the skin soft. Rather, "for purification"; from an Arabic root [Maurer]. Gesenius translates as the Margin, "that thou mightest (be presented to thy parents to) be looked upon," as is customary on the birth of a child.<div eID="gen20216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">salted--</hi>Anciently they rubbed infants with salt to make the skin firm. <div eID="gen20217" type="x-p"/>
entries.c74234b73d30b719bf1849420de5c5c58c51f682: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11207"/><div sID="gen20218" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11207"/><hi type="bold">5. cast ... in ... open field--</hi>The exposure of infants was common in ancient times.<div eID="gen20218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the loathing of thy person--</hi>referring to the unsightly aspect of the exposed infant. Fairbairn translates, "With contempt (or disdainful indifference) of thy life." <div eID="gen20219" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9a0e4c9738ce0c700ef283b36409e096b2265cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11208"/><div sID="gen20220" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11208"/><hi type="bold">6. when I passed by--</hi>as if a traveller.<div eID="gen20220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">polluted in ... blood--</hi>but Piscator, "ready to be trodden on."<div eID="gen20221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20222" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I said--</hi>In contrast to Israel's helplessness stands God's omnipotent word of grace which bids the outcast little one "live."<div eID="gen20222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in thy blood--</hi>Though thou wast foul with blood, I said, "Live" [Grotius]. "Live in thy blood," that is, Live, but live a life exposed to many deaths, as was the case in the beginnings of Israel's national existence, in order to magnify the grace of God [Calvin]. The former view is preferable. Spiritually, till the sinner is made sensible of his abject helplessness, he will not appreciate the provisions of God's grace. <div eID="gen20223" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f8cf8cebb9dd451eb270d93266c88463f1a743f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11209"/><div sID="gen20224" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11209"/><hi type="bold">7. caused ... to multiply--</hi>literally, "I ... made thee a myriad."<div eID="gen20224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bud of ... field--</hi>the produce of the field. In two hundred fifty years they increased from seventy-five persons to eight hundred thousand (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.14">Ac 7:14</reference>) [Calvin]. But see <reference osisRef="Exod.12.37">Ex 12:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.38">38</reference>.<div eID="gen20225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">excellent ornaments--</hi>literally, "ornament of ornaments."<div eID="gen20226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">naked ... bare--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.2.3">Ho 2:3</reference>). Literally, "nakedness ... bareness" itself; more emphatic. <div eID="gen20227" type="x-p"/>
entries.dcf4303f567cbad8e133899bafb2ade6ca301ed5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11210"/><div sID="gen20228" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11210"/><hi type="bold">8. thy time of love--</hi>literally, "loves" (compare <reference osisRef="Song.2.10-Song.2.13">So 2:10-13</reference>). Thou wast of marriageable age, but none was willing to marry thee, naked as thou wast. I then regarded thee with a look of grace when the full time of thy deliverance was come (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.13">Ge 15:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.6">Ac 7:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.7">7</reference>). It is not she that makes the advance to God, but God to her; she has nothing to entitle her to such notice, yet He regards her not with mere benevolence, but with love, such as one cherishes to the person of his wife (<reference osisRef="Song.1.3-Song.1.6">So 1:3-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jr 31:3</reference>; Mal 1:2).<div eID="gen20228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spread my skirt over thee--</hi>the mode of espousals (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.9">Ru 3:9</reference>). I betrothed thee (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.37">De 4:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.10.15">10:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Ho 11:1</reference>). The cloak is often used as a bed coverlet in the East. God explains what He means, "I entered into ... covenant with thee," that is, at Sinai. So Israel became "the wife of God's covenant" (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">Jr 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.19">Ho 2:19</reference>, 20; Mal 2:14).<div eID="gen20229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20230" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou ... mine--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Ex 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jr 2:2</reference>). <div eID="gen20230" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb29d6a27cf8646b5db41d8f8771be133d41f323: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11211"/><div sID="gen20231" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11211"/><hi type="bold">9. washed I thee--</hi>as brides used to pass through a preparatory purification (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.12">Es 2:12</reference>). So Israel, before the giving of the law at Sinai (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.14">Ex 19:14</reference>); "Moses sanctified the people, and they washed their clothes." So believers (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1Co 6:11</reference>).<div eID="gen20231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20232" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oil--</hi>emblem of the Levitical priesthood, the type of Messiah (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>). <div eID="gen20232" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c65a6ab2dd4d59733b5c37ad72a2d1b5c6f3758: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11212"/><div sID="gen20233" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11212"/>10. <reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">Psa 45:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">14</reference>, similarly describes the Church (Israel, the appointed mother of Christendom) adorned as a bride (so <reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Is 61:10</reference>). It is Messiah who provides the wedding garment (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Re 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">19:8</reference>).<div eID="gen20233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20234" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">badgers' skin--</hi>tahash; others translate, "seal skins." They formed the over-covering of the tabernacle, which was, as it were, the nuptial tent of God and Israel (<reference osisRef="Exod.26.14">Ex 26:14</reference>), and the material of the shoes worn by the Hebrews on festival days. (See on <reference osisRef="Exod.25.5">Ex 25:5</reference>).<div eID="gen20234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fine linen--</hi>used by the priests (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.10">Le 6:10</reference>); emblem of purity. <div eID="gen20235" type="x-p"/>
entries.d82d5863b153c8d20a73a71c3cff318f557472c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11213"/><div sID="gen20236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11213"/>11. The marriage gifts to Rebekah (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.22">Ge 24:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.47">47</reference>). <div eID="gen20236" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f1a253b7cd6eeaa82b0ab790fb9171367b7d1c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11214"/><div sID="gen20237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11214"/><hi type="bold">12. jewel on thy forehead--</hi>rather, "a ring in thy nose" (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.21">Is 3:21</reference>).<div eID="gen20237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a crown--</hi>at once the badge of a bride, and of her being made a queen, as being consort of the King; the very name Israel meaning "a prince of God." So they are called "a kingdom of priests" (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Ex 19:6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Re 1:6</reference>). Though the external blessings bestowed on Israel were great, yet not these, but the internal and spiritual, form the main reference in the kingly marriage to which Israel was advanced. <div eID="gen20238" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e690bf100293a3ab5842ccb0ae0fd713895f600: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11215"/><div sID="gen20239" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11215"/><hi type="bold">13. flour ... honey ... oil--</hi>These three mixed form the sweetest cakes; not dry bread and leeks as in Egypt. From raiment He passes to food (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">De 32:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen20239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exceeding beautiful--</hi><reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>, the city; also, <reference osisRef="Ps.29.2">Psa 29:2</reference>, the temple.<div eID="gen20240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prosper into a kingdom--</hi>exercising empire over surrounding nations. <div eID="gen20241" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f1163e84246534d4e1cc991ed6408d2afd32285: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11216"/><div sID="gen20242" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11216"/><hi type="bold">14. thy renown ... among ... heathen--</hi>The theocracy reached its highest point under Solomon, when distant potentates heard of his "fame" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.1">1Ki 10:1</reference>, &c.), for example, the queen of Sheba, Hiram, &c. (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">La 2:15</reference>).<div eID="gen20242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20243" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my comeliness--</hi>It was not thine own, but imparted by Me. <div eID="gen20243" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4bd15544a6e55f8e5c78d2e42d74a16f5435ad7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11217"/><div sID="gen20244" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11217"/>15. Instead of attributing the glory of her privileges and gifts to God, Israel prided herself on them as her own (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">De 32:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jr 7:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mi 3:11</reference>), and then wantonly devoted them to her idols (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.8">Ho 2:8</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.15.12">Lu 15:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.15.13">13</reference>).<div eID="gen20244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">playedst ... harlot because of thy renown--</hi>"didst play the wanton upon thy name" [Fairbairn], namely, by allowing thy renown to lead thee into idolatry and leagues with idolaters (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.21">Is 1:21</reference>; 57:8; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.2">Jr 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.6">6</reference>). English Version is better, "because of thy renown," that is, relying on it; answering to "thou didst trust in thine own beauty."<div eID="gen20245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his it was--</hi>Thy beauty was yielded up to every passer-by. Israel's zest for the worship of foul idols was but an anxiety to have the approbation of heaven for their carnal lusts, of which the idols were the personification; hence, too, their tendency to wander from Jehovah, who was a restraint on corrupt nature. <div eID="gen20246" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8ac29d0dc60df415bc46578f4c452342f54863b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11218"/><div sID="gen20247" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11218"/><hi type="bold">16. deckedst ... with divers colours--</hi>or, "didst make ... of divers colors" [Fairbairn]; the metaphor and the literal are here mixed. The high places whereon they sacrificed to Astarte are here compared to tents of divers colors, which an impudent harlot would spread to show her house was open to all [Calvin]. Compare as to "woven hangings for Astarte" (the right translation for "grove") <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.7">2Ki 23:7</reference>.<div eID="gen20247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the like ... shall not come, neither shall ... be--</hi>rather, "have not come, nor shall be." These thy doings are unparalleled in the past, and shall be so in the future. <div eID="gen20248" type="x-p"/>
entries.d7f094d76789c565c67e568581f04ff4db0b3195: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11219"/><div sID="gen20249" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11219"/><hi type="bold">17. my gold ... my silver--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hag.2.8">Hag 2:8</reference>).<div eID="gen20249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">images of men--</hi>rather, "of the phallus," the Hindu lingam, or membrum virile [Havernick], deified as the emblem of fecundity; man making his lust his god. English Version, however, is appropriate; Israel being represented as a woman playing the harlot with "male images," that is, images of male gods, as distinguished from female deities. <div eID="gen20250" type="x-p"/>
entries.df51ca2373422ff8a6e53a943e7b01e61da6f591: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11220"/><div sID="gen20251" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11220"/><hi type="bold">18. tookest thy ... garments ... coveredst them--</hi>that is, the idols, as if an adulteress were to cover her paramours with garments which she had received from the liberality of her husband.<div eID="gen20251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20252" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my oil--</hi>the holy anointing oil sacred to God (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.22-Exod.30.25">Ex 30:22-25</reference>). Also that used in sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.1">Le 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>). <div eID="gen20252" type="x-p"/>
entries.34fadf4341e95309865de7aa6596969dd54f052b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11221"/><div sID="gen20253" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11221"/><hi type="bold">19. My meat ... I gave--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.2.8">Ho 2:8</reference>).<div eID="gen20253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20254" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set it before them--</hi>as a minchah or "meat offering" (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.1">Le 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen20254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20255" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a sweet savour--</hi>literally, "a savor of rest," that is, whereby they might be propitiated, and be at peace ("rest") with you; how ridiculous to seek to propitiate gods of wood!<div eID="gen20255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thus it was--</hi>The fact cannot be denied, for I saw it, and say it was so, saith Jehovah. <div eID="gen20256" type="x-p"/>
entries.025289e7d250ffa4f7f0410b311631c9e9f550e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11222"/><div sID="gen20257" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11222"/><hi type="bold">20-21. sons and ... daughters borne unto me--</hi>Though "thy children," yet they belong "unto Me," rather than to thee, for they were born under the immutable covenant with Israel, which even Israel's sin could not set aside, and they have received the sign of adoption as Mine, namely, circumcision. This aggravates the guilt of sacrificing them to Molech.<div eID="gen20257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be devoured--</hi>not merely to pass through the fire, as sometimes children were made to do (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">Le 18:21</reference>) without hurt, but to pass through so as to be made the food of the flame in honor of idols (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.57.5">Is 57:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.31">Jr 7:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.19.5">Jr 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.35">Jr 32:35</reference>).<div eID="gen20258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20259" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Is this of thy whoredoms a small matter, that thou hast slain my children--</hi>rather, "Were thy whoredoms a small matter (that is, not enough, but) that thou hast slain (that is, must also slay)," &c. As if thy unchastity was not enough, thou hast added this unnatural and sacrilegious cruelty (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.7">Mi 6:7</reference>). <div eID="gen20259" type="x-p"/>
entries.78aec44cff896e0903fc43f47084f04d38abb949: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11223"/><div sID="gen20260" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11223"/><hi type="bold">22. not remembered ... youth--</hi>Forgetfulness of God's love is the source of all sins. Israel forgot her deliverance by God in the infancy of her national life. See <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.43">Eze 16:43</reference>, to which <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.60">Eze 16:60</reference> forms a lovely contrast (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jr 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Ho 11:1</reference>). <div eID="gen20260" type="x-p"/>
entries.52faf6d7e07d6b6a06301f6a63479024ede17354: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11224"/><div sID="gen20261" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11224"/><hi type="bold">23. woe, woe unto thee, &c.--</hi>This parenthetical exclamation has an awful effect coming like a lightning flash of judgment amidst the black clouds of Israel's guilt. <div eID="gen20261" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8511a5ac06541577ec0db01a58fec38d6748d16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11225"/><div sID="gen20262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11225"/><hi type="bold">24. eminent place--</hi>rather, "a fornication-chamber," often connected with the impure rites of idolatry; spiritual fornication, on "an eminent place," answering to "fornication-chamber," is mainly meant, with an allusion also to the literal fornication associated with it (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.20">Jr 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">3:2</reference>). <div eID="gen20262" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4f6fd57a5c777abf75a3b3fb32b174c903208df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11226"/><div sID="gen20263" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11226"/><hi type="bold">25. at every head of the way--</hi>in the most frequented places (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.14">Pr 9:14</reference>).<div eID="gen20263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy beauty ... abhorred, ... opened ... feet to every one--</hi>The wanton advances were all on Israel's part; the idolatrous nations yielded to her nothing in return. She had yielded so much that, like a worn-out prostitute, her tempters became weary of her. When the Church lowers her testimony for God to the carnal tastes of the world, with a view to conciliation, she loses everything and gains nothing. <div eID="gen20264" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fde1d61b6f4df79816dd19543e866f92c635d07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11227"/><div sID="gen20265" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11227"/><hi type="bold">26. fornication with ... Egyptians--</hi>alliances with Egypt, cemented by sharing their idolatries.<div eID="gen20265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20266" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">great of flesh--</hi>of powerful virile parts; figuratively for the gross and lustful religion of Egypt (for example, Isis, &c.), which alone could satisfy the abominable lust of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.7">Eze 20:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.19">23:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.21">20, 21</reference>).<div eID="gen20266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to provoke me--</hi>wantonly and purposely. <div eID="gen20267" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c716a690bf9f56ec81b0b66d22996711c92d34b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11228"/><div sID="gen20268" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11228"/>27. The consequent judgments, which, however, proved of no avail in reforming the people (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Is 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.3">Jr 5:3</reference>).<div eID="gen20268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delivered thee unto ... Philistines--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.6">2Ki 16:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.18">2Ch 28:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.19">19</reference>).<div eID="gen20269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ashamed of thy lewd way--</hi>The Philistines were less wanton in idolatry, in that they did not, like Israel, adopt the idols of every foreign country but were content with their own (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.57">Eze 16:57</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.11">Jr 2:11</reference>). <div eID="gen20270" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d271208ac92a42abaa73868869597bfdc34897e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11229"/><div sID="gen20271" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11229"/><hi type="bold">28. unsatiable--</hi>Not satisfied with whoredoms with neighbors, thou hast gone off to the distant Assyrians, that is, hast sought a league with them, and with it adopted their idolatries. <div eID="gen20271" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c978a36eebc8a01d3cc5f8a83099df94145131c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11230"/><div sID="gen20272" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11230"/><hi type="bold">29. multiplied ... fornication in ... Canaan unto Chaldea--</hi>Thou hast multiplied thy idolatries "in Canaan" by sending "unto Chaldea" to borrow from thence the Chaldean rites, to add to the abominations already practised "in Canaan," before the carrying away of Jehoiachin to Chaldea. The name "Canaan" is used to imply that they had made Judea as much the scene of abominations as it was in the days of the corrupt Canaanites. The land had become utterly Canaanitish (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.14">Eze 23:14</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen20272" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c3bbcb3f618b49bda87af4643a5e00678bcf5f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11231"/><div sID="gen20273" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11231"/><hi type="bold">30. weak ... heart--</hi>Sin weakens the intellect ("heart") as, on the contrary, "the way of the Lord is strength to the upright" (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.29">Pr 10:29</reference>). <div eID="gen20273" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3158f082394d647af9a40d5ceff0d5e187d1048: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11232"/><div sID="gen20274" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11232"/>31. Repetition of <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.24">Eze 16:24</reference>.<div eID="gen20274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20275" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not ... as ... harlot ... thou scornest hire--</hi>Unlike an ordinary harlot thou dost prostitute thy person gratis, merely to satisfy thy lust. Jerome translates, "Thou hast not been as a harlot in scorning (that is, who ordinarily scorns) a hire offered," in order to get a larger one: nay, thou hast offered hire thyself to thy lovers (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.33">Eze 16:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.34">34</reference>). But these verses show English Version to be preferable, for they state that Israel prostituted herself, not merely for any small reward without demanding more, but for "no reward." <div eID="gen20275" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f6dd10216a459316b7f87d2a730232a4cb6f75e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11233"/><div sID="gen20276" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11233"/><hi type="bold">32. instead of her husband--</hi>referring to <reference osisRef="Num.5.19">Nu 5:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.20.29">20, 29</reference>. Fairbairn translates, "whilst under her husband." <div eID="gen20276" type="x-p"/>
entries.db057fd05d4d40c1c840ea28e5d2f8e8d54fbd43: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11234"/><div sID="gen20277" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11234"/>33-34. Israel hired her paramours, instead of being, like other harlots, hired by them; she also followed them without their following her. <div eID="gen20277" type="x-p"/>
entries.5044351ea08b8388e2a1ffed0d49c084a33d963e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11235"/><div sID="gen20278" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11235"/>35. Here begins the threat of wrath to be poured out on her. <div eID="gen20278" type="x-p"/>
entries.efd86358410999f6bdb1c64b2ba228e6ef64d670: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11236"/><div sID="gen20279" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11236"/><hi type="bold">36. filthiness--</hi>literally, "brass"; metaphor for the lowest part of the person [Calvin]. English Version is better: thy filthy lewdness is poured out without restraint (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.13.27">Jr 13:27</reference>). As silver is an emblem of purity, brass typifies "filthiness," because it easily contracts rust. Henderson explains it, "Because thy money was lavished on thy lovers" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.31">Eze 16:31</reference>, 33, 34).<div eID="gen20279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blood of thy children--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.20">Eze 16:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.34">Jr 2:34</reference>). <div eID="gen20280" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0a188e6bcc5c66d6d384239b7fae678b483fe3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11237"/><div sID="gen20281" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11237"/><hi type="bold">37. thy lovers--</hi>the Chaldeans and the Assyrians. The law of retribution is the more signally exemplified by God employing, as His instruments of judgment on Israel, those very nations whose alliance and idols Israel had so eagerly sought, besides giving her up to those who had been always her enemies. "God will make him, who leaves God for the world, disgraced even in the eyes of the world, and indeed the more so the nearer he formerly stood to Himself" [Hengstenberg], (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">Is 47:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.13.26">Jr 13:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.12">Ho 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.5">Na 3:5</reference>).<div eID="gen20281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20282" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... thou hast hated--</hi>the Edomites and Philistines; also Moab and Ammon especially (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.3">De 23:3</reference>).<div eID="gen20282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20283" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ... will discover thy nakedness--</hi>punishment in kind, as she had "discovered her nakedness through whoredoms" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.36">Eze 16:36</reference>); the sin and its penalty corresponded. I will expose thee to public infamy. <div eID="gen20283" type="x-p"/>
entries.6403670539feeab42d3de22636234f135d90715d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11238"/><div sID="gen20284" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11238"/><hi type="bold">38-40. judge thee, as women that break wedlock--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.20.10">Le 20:10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.2">Eze 16:2</reference>). In the case of individual adulteresses, stoning was the penalty (<reference osisRef="John.8.4">Joh 8:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.8.5">5</reference>). In the case of communities, the sword. Also apostasy (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.10">De 13:10</reference>) and sacrificing children to Molech (<reference osisRef="Lev.20.1-Lev.20.5">Le 20:1-5</reference>) incurred stoning. Thus the penalty was doubly due to Israel; so the other which was decreed against an apostate city (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.15">De 13:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.16">16</reference>) is added, "they shall stone thee with stones and thrust thee through with ... swords." The Chaldeans hurled stones on Jerusalem at the siege and slew with the sword on its capture.<div eID="gen20284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20285" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shed blood ... judged--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Ge 9:6</reference>).<div eID="gen20285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20286" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">jealousy--</hi>image taken from the fury of a husband in jealousy shedding the blood of an unfaithful wife, such as Israel had been towards God, her husband spiritually. Literally, "I will make thee (to become) blood of fury and jealousy." <div eID="gen20286" type="x-p"/>
entries.50786a736f0a626de8bc3f9165d978e442c5142c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11241"/><div sID="gen20291" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11241"/>41. The result of the awful judgment shall be, when divine vengeance has run its course, it shall cease.<div eID="gen20291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20292" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burn--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.13.16">De 13:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.9">2Ki 25:9</reference>).<div eID="gen20292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20293" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">women--</hi>the surrounding Gentile nations to whom thou shalt be an object of mocking (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>).<div eID="gen20293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will cause thee to cease ... harlot--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.27">Eze 23:27</reference>). Thou shalt no longer be able to play the harlot through My judgments.<div eID="gen20294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20295" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou ... shall give ... no hire ... any more--</hi>Thou shalt have none to give. <div eID="gen20295" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f77d9bf800e9742e51d46d18c2db3596686c41e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11242"/><div sID="gen20296" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11242"/><hi type="bold">42. my fury ... rest--</hi>when My justice has exacted the full penalty commensurate with thy awful guilt (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.13">Eze 5:13</reference>). It is not a mitigation of the penalty that is here foretold, but such an utter destruction of all the guilty that there shall be no need of further punishment [Calvin]. <div eID="gen20296" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c2d80ed132c6427fd73bd565f567d9056e7b91a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11243"/><div sID="gen20297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11243"/>43. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.22">Eze 16:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.42">Psa 78:42</reference>). In gratitude for God's favors to her in her early history.<div eID="gen20297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fretted me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">Is 63:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.30">Ep 4:30</reference>).<div eID="gen20298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20299" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shalt not commit this lewdness above all thine abominations--</hi>that is, this the wickedness (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.5.8">Zec 5:8</reference>), peculiarly hateful to God, namely, spiritual unchastity or idolatry, over and "above" (that is, besides) all thine other abominations. I will put it out of thy power to commit it by cutting thee off. Fairbairn translates, "I will not do what is scandalous (namely, encouraging thee in thy sin by letting it pass with impunity) upon all thine abominations"; referring to <reference osisRef="Lev.19.29">Le 19:29</reference>, the conduct of a father who encouraged his daughter in harlotry. English Version is much better. <div eID="gen20299" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce20a7303f505d9f61a5aa4988644be5f26a01fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11244"/><div sID="gen20300" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11244"/><hi type="bold">44. As ... mother ... her daughter--</hi>"Is," and "so is," are not in the original; the ellipsis gives the proverb (but two words in the Hebrew) epigrammatic brevity. Jerusalem proved herself a true daughter of the Hittite mother in sin (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.3">Eze 16:3</reference>). <div eID="gen20300" type="x-p"/>
entries.64a7d46d5739ab3bd9e425dd7c2f7bba6dad05d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11245"/><div sID="gen20301" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11245"/><hi type="bold">45. mother's ... that loatheth her husband--</hi>that is, God ("haters of God," <reference osisRef="Rom.1.30">Ro 1:30</reference>); therefore the knowledge of the true God had originally been in Canaan, handed down from Noah (hence we find Melchisedek, king of Salem, in Canaan, "priest of the most high God," <reference osisRef="Gen.14.18">Ge 14:18</reference>), but Canaan apostatized from it; this was what constituted the blackness of the Canaanites' guilt.<div eID="gen20301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20302" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loathed ... children--</hi>whom she put to death in honor of Saturn; a practice common among the Phoenicians.<div eID="gen20302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20303" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sister of thy sisters--</hi>Thou art akin in guilt to Samaria and Sodom, to which thou art akin by birth. Moab and Ammon, the incestuous children of Lot, nephew of Abraham, Israel's progenitor, had their origin from Sodom; so Sodom might be called Judah's sister. Samaria, answering to the ten tribes of Israel, is, of course, sister to Judah. <div eID="gen20303" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2e13b4e126d1983c85a6b607c9378e6dac4255d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11246"/><div sID="gen20304" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11246"/><hi type="bold">46. elder sister ... Samaria--</hi>older than Sodom, to whom Judah was less nearly related by kindred than she was to Samaria. Sodom is therefore called her younger sister; Samaria, her "elder sister" [Grotius]. Samaria is called the "elder," because in a moral respect more nearly related to Judah [Fairbairn]. Samaria had made the calves at Dan and Beth-el in imitation of the cherubim.<div eID="gen20304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20305" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her daughters--</hi>the inferior towns subject to Samaria (compare <reference osisRef="Num.21.25">Nu 21:25</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen20305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">left--</hi>The Orientals faced the east in marking the directions of the sky; thus the north was "left," the south "right."<div eID="gen20306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20307" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sodom ... daughters--</hi>Ammon and Moab, offshoots from Sodom; also the towns subject to it. <div eID="gen20307" type="x-p"/>
entries.feffd580d509d10d1aa0f837e84004c4c79c8b40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11247"/><div sID="gen20308" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11247"/><hi type="bold">47. their abominations--</hi>Milcom and Chemosh, the "abominations of Ammon and Moab" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.5">1Ki 11:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen20308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corrupted more than they--</hi>So it is expressly recorded of Manasseh (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.9">2Ki 21:9</reference>). <div eID="gen20309" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9abf2cf6b591553ffbb619b967674ded8de4e25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11248"/><div sID="gen20310" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11248"/><hi type="bold">48. Sodom--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.11.24">Mt 11:24</reference>). Judah's guilt was not positively, but relatively, greater than Sodom's; because it was in the midst of such higher privileges, and such solemn warnings; a fortiori, the guilt of unbelievers in the midst of the highest of all lights, namely, the Gospel, is the greatest. <div eID="gen20310" type="x-p"/>
entries.8398485a80593fb461365a72d33ef45c7e802a0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11249"/><div sID="gen20311" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11249"/><hi type="bold">49. pride--</hi>inherited by Moab, her offspring (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Is 16:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.26">Jr 48:26</reference>), and by Ammon (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.4">Jr 49:4</reference>). God, the heart-searcher, here specifies as Sodom's sin, not merely her notorious lusts, but the secret spring of them, "pride" flowing from "fullness of bread," caused by the fertility of the soil (<reference osisRef="Gen.13.10">Ge 13:10</reference>), and producing "idleness."<div eID="gen20311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20312" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abundance of idleness--</hi>literally, "the secure carelessness of ease" or idleness.<div eID="gen20312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither did she strengthen ... the poor--</hi>Pride is always cruel; it arrogates to itself all things, and despises brethren, for whose needs it therefore has no feeling; as Moab had not for the outcast Jews (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.3">Is 16:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.27">Jr 48:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.16.19-Luke.16.21">Lu 16:19-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.1-Jas.5.5">Jas 5:1-5</reference>). <div eID="gen20313" type="x-p"/>
entries.6719774807dc8146f3cdbdcec7a5590b28589253: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11250"/><div sID="gen20314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11250"/><hi type="bold">50. haughty--</hi>puffed up with prosperity.<div eID="gen20314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abomination before me--</hi>"sinners before the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Gen.13.13">Ge 13:13</reference>); said of those whose sin is so heinous as to cry out to God for immediate judgments; presumptuous sins, daring God to the face (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.20">Ge 18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.19.5">19:5</reference>).<div eID="gen20315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I took them away--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.19.24">Ge 19:24</reference>).<div eID="gen20316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20317" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as I saw good--</hi>rather, "according to what I saw"; referring to <reference osisRef="Gen.18.21">Ge 18:21</reference>, where God says, "I will go down, and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry of it which is come unto Me." <div eID="gen20317" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed3b2f8606853d2d962aacd0a0e96b66bbf8eebd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11251"/><div sID="gen20318" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11251"/><hi type="bold">51. Samaria--</hi>the kingdom of the ten tribes of Israel less guilty than Judah; for Judah betrayed greater ingratitude, having greater privileges, namely, the temple, the priesthood, and the regular order of kings.<div eID="gen20318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">justified thy sisters--</hi>made them appear almost innocent by comparison with thy guilt (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.11">Jr 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.12.41">Mt 12:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.42">42</reference>). <div eID="gen20319" type="x-p"/>
entries.f01fd6d40ab35c7954f123c484936a3360e8b78f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11252"/><div sID="gen20320" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11252"/><hi type="bold">52. Thou ... which hast judged ... bear thine own--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.7.1">Mt 7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.2">2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.1">Ro 2:1</reference>, 17-23). Judah had judged Sodom (representing "the heathen nations") and Samaria (Israel), saying they were justly punished, as if she herself was innocent (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.2">Lu 13:2</reference>).<div eID="gen20320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy shame--</hi>ignominious punishment. <div eID="gen20321" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf5b84d236b8dd4dc9d737c9f44b94e72e793cab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11253"/><div sID="gen20322" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11253"/>53. Here follows a promise of restoration. Even the sore chastisements coming on Judah would fail to reform its people; God's returning goodness alone would effect this, to show how entirely of grace was to be their restoration. The restoration of her erring sisters is mentioned before hers, even as their punishment preceded her punishment; so all self-boasting is excluded [Fairbairn]. "Ye shall, indeed, at some time or other return, but Moab and Ammon shall return with you, and some of the ten tribes" [Grotius].<div eID="gen20322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring again ... captivity--</hi>that is, change the affliction into prosperity (so <reference osisRef="Job.42.10">Job 42:10</reference>). Sodom itself was not so restored (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.16">Jr 20:16</reference>), but Ammon and Moab (her representatives, as sprung from Lot who dwelt in Sodom) were (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.47">Jr 48:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.6">49:6</reference>); probably most of the ten tribes and the adjoining nations, Ammon and Moab, &c., were in part restored under Cyrus; but the full realization of the restoration is yet future; the heathen nations to be brought to Christ being typified by "Sodom," whose sins they now reproduce (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">De 32:32</reference>).<div eID="gen20323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20324" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">captivity of thy captives--</hi>literally, "of thy captivities." However, the gracious promise rather begins with the "nevertheless" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.60">Eze 16:60</reference>), not here; for <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.59">Eze 16:59</reference> is a threat, not a promise. The sense here thus is, Thou shalt be restored when Sodom and Samaria are, but not till then (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.55">Eze 16:55</reference>), that is, never. This applies to the guilty who should be utterly destroyed (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.41">Eze 16:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.42">42</reference>); but it does not contradict the subsequent promise of restoration to their posterity (<reference osisRef="Num.14.29-Num.14.33">Nu 14:29-33</reference>), and to the elect remnant of grace [Calvin]. <div eID="gen20324" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe9db708a602375b38978d0e67a0f426641e59ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11254"/><div sID="gen20325" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11254"/><hi type="bold">54. bear thine own shame--</hi>by being put on a level with those whom thou hast so much despised.<div eID="gen20325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou art a comfort unto them--</hi>since they see thee as miserable as themselves. It is a kind of melancholy "comfort" to those chastised to see others as sorely punished as themselves (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.22">Eze 14:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.23">23</reference>). <div eID="gen20326" type="x-p"/>
entries.83bcdfa7107e272b1953b213dca35e4fe56e5c9c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11255"/><div sID="gen20327" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11255"/>55. (See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.53">Eze 16:53</reference>). <div eID="gen20327" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b53a12e25ed74a3b2ba13d9e4e2b2141f6ce8db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11256"/><div sID="gen20328" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11256"/><hi type="bold">56. Sodom was not mentioned--</hi>literally, "was not for a report." Thou didst not deign to mention her name as if her case could possibly apply as a warning to thee, but it did apply (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.6">2Pe 2:6</reference>). <div eID="gen20328" type="x-p"/>
entries.8424d60e54502ab206d08cbb3851174e3fe12b68: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11257"/><div sID="gen20329" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11257"/><hi type="bold">57. Before thy wickedness was discovered--</hi>manifested to all, namely, by the punishment inflicted on thee.<div eID="gen20329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20330" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy reproach of ... Syria and ... Philistines--</hi>the indignity and injuries done thee by Syria and the Philistines (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.5">2Ki 16:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.18">2Ch 28:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.11">Is 9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen20330" type="x-p"/>
entries.992a904839c327f89ff45e19a4f47ad39a57aa55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11258"/><div sID="gen20331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11258"/><hi type="bold">58. borne thy lewdness--</hi>that is, the punishment of it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.49">Eze 23:49</reference>). I do not treat thee with excessive rigor. Thy sin and punishment are exactly commensurate. <div eID="gen20331" type="x-p"/>
entries.3bc5693f87da78e7d0507f3d4c023686d17beb52: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11259"/><div sID="gen20332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11259"/><hi type="bold">59. the oath--</hi>the covenant between God and Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.12">De 29:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.14">14</reference>). As thou hast despised it, so will I despise thee. No covenant is one-sided; where Israel broke faith, God's promise of favor ceased. <div eID="gen20332" type="x-p"/>
entries.32c63c13ea944d6110a0a9d86ea4f673d287cc00: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11260"/><div sID="gen20333" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11260"/>60. The promise here bursts forth unexpectedly like the sun from the dark clouds. With all her forgetfulness of God, God still remembers her; showing that her redemption is altogether of grace. Contrast "I will remember," with "thou hast not remembered" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.22">Eze 16:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.43">43</reference>); also "My covenant," with "Thy covenant" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.61">Eze 16:61</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.45">Psa 106:45</reference>); then the effect produced on her is (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.63">Eze 16:63</reference>) "that thou mayest remember." God's promise was one of promise and of grace. The law, in its letter, was Israel's (thy) covenant, and in this restricted view was long subsequent (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.17">Ga 3:17</reference>). Israel interpreted it as a covenant of works, which she while boasting of, failed to fulfil, and so fell under its condemnation (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.3">2Co 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">6</reference>). The law, in its spirit, contains the germ of the Gospel; the New Testament is the full development of the Old, the husk of the outer form being laid aside when the inner spirit was fulfilled in Messiah. God's covenant with Israel, in the person of Abraham, was the reason why, notwithstanding all her guilt, mercy was, and is, in store for her. Therefore the heathen or Gentile nations must come to her for blessings, not she to them.<div eID="gen20333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting covenant--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.26">Eze 37:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Is 55:3</reference>). The temporary forms of the law were to be laid aside, that in its permanent and "everlasting" spirit it might be established (Jr 31:31-37; 32:40; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.4">50:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.8.8-Heb.8.13">He 8:8-13</reference>). <div eID="gen20334" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a91b3370e6346e5739c81acf8ad2fc11704e908: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11261"/><div sID="gen20335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11261"/><hi type="bold">61. thou shalt remember--</hi>It is God who first remembers her before she remembers Him and her own ways before Him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.60">Eze 16:60</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.43">Eze 20:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.31">36:31</reference>).<div eID="gen20335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ashamed--</hi>the fruit of repentance (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.10">2Co 7:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.11">11</reference>). None please God unless those who displease themselves; a foretaste of the Gospel (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.9-Luke.18.14">Lu 18:9-14</reference>).<div eID="gen20336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20337" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will give them unto thee for daughters--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Is 54:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.3">60:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.26">Ga 4:26</reference>, &c.). All the heathen nations, not merely Sodom and Samaria, are meant by "thy sisters, elder and younger." In Jerusalem first, individual believers were gathered into the elect Church. From Jerusalem the Gospel went forth to gather in individuals of the Gentiles; and Judah with Jerusalem shall also be the first nation which, as such, shall be converted to Christ; and to her the other nations shall attach themselves as believers in Messiah, Jerusalem's King (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.2">Psa 110:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>). "The king's daughter" in <reference osisRef="Ps.45.12-Ps.45.14">Psa 45:12-14</reference> is Judah; her "companions," as "the daughter of Tyre," are the nations given to her as converts, here called "daughters."<div eID="gen20337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not by thy covenant--</hi>This does not set aside the Old Testament in its spirit, but in its mere letter on which the Jews had rested, while they broke it: the latter ("thy covenant") was to give place to God's covenant of grace and promise in Christ who "fulfilled" the law. God means, "not that thou on thy part hast stood to the covenant, but that 'I am the Lord, I change not' (Mal 3:6) from My original love to thee in thy youth" (see <reference osisRef="Rom.3.3">Ro 3:3</reference>). <div eID="gen20338" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c48e2f75d4493170ccaacc9df6fdd3c01f5eb15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11262"/><div sID="gen20339" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11262"/>62. (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.19">Ho 2:19</reference>, 20).<div eID="gen20339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20340" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shalt know that I am the Lord--</hi>not, as elsewhere, by the judgments falling on thee, but by My so marvellously restoring thee through grace. <div eID="gen20340" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3ceef1dc7a18bfff37606ff055cca9763e68fa4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11263"/><div sID="gen20341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11263"/><hi type="bold">63. never open thy mouth--</hi>in vindication, or even palliation, of thyself, or expostulation with God for His dealings (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.19">Ro 3:19</reference>), when thou seest thine own exceeding unworthiness, and My superabounding grace which has so wonderfully overcome with love thy sin (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.20">Ro 5:20</reference>). "If we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.31">1Co 11:31</reference>).<div eID="gen20341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all that thou hast done--</hi>enhancing the grace of God which has pardoned so many and so great sins. Nothing so melts into love and humility as the sense of the riches of God's pardoning grace (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.47">Lu 7:47</reference>). <chapter eID="Ezek.16"/>

entries.d2e9d466d86271278bd39f56c39a3f04fd7d381c: <div eID="gen31555" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31556" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31557" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31557" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31556" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31558" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the mercy of God to Jerusalem, (or the Jewish Church and nation), is set forth by the emblem of a person that should take up an exposed infant, bring her up with great tenderness, and afterwards marry her, <reference osisRef="Eze.16.1-Eze.16.14">Eze 16:1-14</reference>. She is then upbraided with her monstrous ingratitude in departing from the worship of God, and polluting herself with the idolatries of the nations around her, under the figure of a woman that proves false to a tender and indulgent husband, vv. 15-52. But, notwithstanding these her heinous provocations, God promises, after she should suffer due correction, to restore her again to his favor, <reference osisRef="Eze.16.53-Eze.16.63">Eze 16:53-63</reference>. The mode of describing apostasy from the true religion to the worship of idols under the emblem of adultery, (a figure very frequent in the sacred canon), is pursued with great force, and at considerable length, both in this and the twenty-third chapter; and is excellently calculated to excite in the Church of God the highest detestation of all false worship.
entries.409891124eab78c436560932b1e61b6fdbb7711f: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31559" type="x-p"/> Cause Jerusalem to know her abominations - And such a revelation of impurity never was seen before or since. Surely the state of the Jews, before the Babylonish captivity, was the most profligate and corrupt of all the nations of the earth. This chapter contains God's manifesto against this most abominable people; and although there are many metaphors here, yet all is not metaphorical. Where there was so much idolatry, there must have been adulteries, fornications, prostitutions, and lewdness of every description. The description of the prophet is sufficiently clear, except where there is a reference to ancient and obsolete customs. What a description of crimes! The sixth satire of Juvenal is its counterpart. General remarks are all that a commentator is justified in bestowing on this very long, very circumstantial, and caustic invective. For its key, see on <reference osisRef="Eze.16.13">Eze 16:13</reference> (note) and <reference osisRef="Eze.16.63">Eze 16:63</reference> (note).
entries.74fb881f72612167269c11f0707539c4b51f7df0: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen31559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31560" type="x-p"/> Thy birth and thy nativity is of the land of Canaan - It would dishonor Abraham to say that you sprung from him: ye are rather Canaanites than Israelites. The Canaanites were accursed; so are ye. <div eID="gen31560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31561" type="x-p"/> Thy father was an Amorite, and thy mother a Hittite - These tribes were the most famous, and probably the most corrupt, of all the Canaanites. So Isaiah calls the princes of Judah rulers of Sodom, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.10">Isa 1:10</reference>; and John the Baptist calls the Pharisees a generation or brood of vipers, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.7">Mat 3:7</reference>. There is a fine specimen of this kind of catachresis in Dido's invective against Aeneas: - <div eID="gen31561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31562" type="x-p"/> Nec tibi Diva parens, generis nec <div eID="gen31562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31563" type="x-p"/> Dardanus auctor, Perflde; sed duris genuit te cautibus horrens <div eID="gen31563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31564" type="x-p"/> Caucasus, Hyrcanaeque admorunt ubera tigres. <div eID="gen31564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31565" type="x-p"/> Aen. lib. 4:365. "False as thou art, and more than false, forsworn; <div eID="gen31565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31566" type="x-p"/> Not sprung from noble blood, nor goddess born: <div eID="gen31566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31567" type="x-p"/> But hewn from hardened entrails of a rock, - <div eID="gen31567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31568" type="x-p"/> And rough Hyrcanian tigers gave thee suck." <div eID="gen31568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31569" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen31569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31570" type="x-p"/> This is strong: but the invective of the prophet exceeds it far. It is the essence of degradation to its subject; and shows the Jews to be as base and contemptible as they were abominable and disgusting.
entries.45d1ddcad91f9babac5c2baeaffa01896b9f641d: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31571" type="x-p"/> As for thy nativity, etc. - This verse refers to what is ordinarily done for every infant on its birth. The umbilical cord, by which it received all its nourishment while in the womb, being no longer necessary, is cut at a certain distance from the abdomen: on this part a knot is tied, which firmly uniting the sides of the tubes, they coalesce, and incarnate together. The extra part of the cord on the outside of the ligature, being cut off from the circulation by which it was originally fed, soon drops off, and the part where the ligature was is called the navel. In many places, when this was done, the infant was plunged into cold water; in all cases washed, and sometimes with a mixture of salt and water, in order to give a greater firmness to the skin, and constringe the pores. The last process was swathing the body, to support mechanically the tender muscles till they should acquire sufficient strength to support the body. But among savages this latter process is either wholly neglected, or done very slightly: and the less it is done, the better for the infant; as this kind of unnatural compression greatly impedes the circulation of the blood, the pulsation of the heart, and the due inflation of the lungs; respiration, in many cases, being rendered oppressive by the tightness of these bandages.
entries.0dce493d9e822a233076216b5b68d327b07d7043: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31572" type="x-p"/> Thou wast cast out in the open field - This is an allusion to the custom of some heathen and barbarous nations, who exposed those children in the open fields to be devoured by wild beasts who had any kind of deformity, or whom they could not support.
entries.bd676d6fa6c67d922997e788669caa7d8b09b12f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31573" type="x-p"/> I said - Live - I received the exposed child from the death that awaited it, while in such a state as rendered it at once an object of horror, and also of compassion. - Modo primos Edere vagitus, et adhuc a matre rubentem.
entries.922f72fb947a782ef38a336203cb6bcccf5099d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen31573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31574" type="x-p"/> Was the time of love - Thou wast marriageable. <div eID="gen31574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31575" type="x-p"/> I spread my skirt over thee - I espoused thee. This was one of their initiatory marriage ceremonies. See <reference osisRef="Rut.3.9">Rut 3:9</reference>. <div eID="gen31575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31576" type="x-p"/> I - entered into a covenant with thee - Married thee. Espousing preceded marriage.
